result.title: A forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models: an EFM3D case study for crime scene reconstruction
result.summary: Foundation models increasingly combine geometry, semantics, and spatial context for three-dimensional scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction remains unclear. This study presents a structured forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and demonstrates it using the Egocentric Foundation Model for 3D (EFM3D). Four simulated indoor crime scenes were recorded with Meta Project Aria Gen~1 at Robert Gordon University's East Lodge House forensic training facility. The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability. Across the four scenes, EFM3D generated meshes averaging $12{,}668\pm2{,}430$ vertices and $24{,}838\pm4{,}903$ faces, with 39,529 recorded semantic predictions spanning 21--24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Because reference meshes and expert-labelled 3D ground truth were unavailable, these statistics are treated as descriptive outputs rather than measures of geometric or detection accuracy. Final inference runs processed $1{,}388\pm203$ snippets per scene at $0.69\pm0.01$ samples/s and required $50.77\pm6.12$ minutes per recording. A seven-criterion capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The results position EFM3D as a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture. The framework provides a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in specialised forensic settings.
